title: The Scribe Who Invented Zero
event_summary: A Khmer scribe carved an inscription at a temple near Angkor Borei that contains the earliest known use of zero as a numeral in its own right — not merely a placeholder, but a number within a dated calculation. The inscription, known as K-127, records a land donation and uses the Old Khmer numeral system to write the Saka year 605 (683 AD), embedding a dot-symbol for zero in a fully positional decimal number. This predates the earliest surviving Indian zero-as-numeral inscription by nearly a century.
why_forgotten: The inscription was discovered in the 1930s by French archaeologist George Cœdès, but the significance was overshadowed by the dominant narrative crediting India alone for zero's invention. During the Khmer Rouge era (1975–1979), the original stele vanished and was presumed destroyed, removing the physical evidence from scholarly debate. It was only rediscovered in a warehouse near Angkor Borei in 2015, reigniting interest in Southeast Asia's foundational role in mathematics.
why_it_matters: Every digital device, every line of code, and every financial transaction depends on zero functioning as a true number within a positional system — not just a blank space. The K-127 stele suggests that the conceptual leap making zero a number may have emerged from the intellectual cross-pollination between Indian and Southeast Asian civilizations, challenging the Eurocentric and India-centric narratives of mathematical progress and revealing the Khmer world as a crucible of one of humanity's most consequential abstractions.
